card: Paper card. Question: Can configurational entropy be engineered to stabilize a single-phase solid solution in a five-component oxide system where the constituent binary oxides do not form solid solutions, and can this transition be reversed?. System: Equimolar mixture of MgO, CoO, NiO, CuO, and ZnO (labeled E1). Processing: Solid-state synthesis: powders milled for 2 h, pressed into pellets at 31,000 N, fired in air at temperatures ranging from 700 to 1,100 °C with 50 °C increments, and quenched; thin films prepared via pulsed laser deposition at 600 °C with 3 J cm⁻² energy density.. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring phase evolution from 700 to 1,100 °C; differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ XRD at 5 °C min⁻¹; EXAFS at Advanced Photon Source 12-BM-B; STEM-EDS analysis at 200 kV.. Findings: Full conversion to a single-phase rocksalt structure occurs between 850 and 900 °C, with no additional peaks observed above this range.; Removing any single component from the five-component mixture results in a multiphase material when equilibrated at 875 °C for 12 h.; Deviations from equimolarity by ±2, ±6, and ±10% increase the transition temperature to single phase, confirming the entropic driving force.; The phase transformation from multiphase to single phase is endothermic, with a measured enthalpy change of approximately 12 kJ mol⁻¹ (±2 kJ mol⁻¹).; EXAFS data shows cation-to-anion first-neighbour distances are identical within ±0.01 Å for Zn, Ni, Cu, and Co, consistent with random distribution.; STEM-EDS mapping reveals chemically and structurally homogeneous material with no evidence of phase separation or clustering at the atomic scale.; A small mass loss of approximately 1.5% occurs at the transition due to the reduction of 3+ to 2+ cations during the conversion of spinel intermediates to rocksalt.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high configurational entropy of the five-component equimolar mixture overcomes the positive enthalpic penalties associated with structural transitions (specifically for CuO and ZnO) and mixing, stabilizing the single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. The entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy becomes dominant, driving the reversible transition from a multiphase state to a random solid solution where cations occupy a single sublattice homogeneously.. Limitations: The authors note that quantitative calorimetry presents challenges, and the assumption of ideal mixing for enthalpy calculations is a simplification; literature reports indicate finite and mixed-sign enthalpies of mixing that are not fully captured by the reference transition enthalpy values.. Future work: The authors propose that entropic stabilization should be explored in other systems with intermediate anions, such as chalcogenides, nitrides, and halides, particularly where covalent character is modest, and call for rigorous theoretical exploration of the crystallographic model where intermediate anions render cation sites energetically equivalent.. Quote: "entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state."

W2261135145.title: Entropy-stabilized oxides

card: Paper card. Question: How does entropy stabilization in transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) influence reversible lithium storage capacity, cycling stability, and the underlying reaction mechanism compared to medium entropy oxides?. System: Transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) with composition (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O; compared to 4-cation medium entropy oxides (MEO) such as (Co0.25Cu0.25Zn0.25Ni0.25)O and (Co0.25Cu0.25Mg0.25Zn0.25)O. Processing: Nebulized Spray Pyrolysis (NSP) at 1150 °C; 4-cation systems required post-annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h under ambient atmosphere; electrodes cast with 63 wt% active material, 22 wt% Super C65, 15 wt% PVA binder. Test conditions: Galvanostatic cycling in Li-metal coin cells, voltage range 0.01–3 V vs. Li+/Li, specific currents from 50 to 3000 mA g−1, room temperature, 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC or EC/EMC electrolyte. Findings: The 5-cation TM-HEO cycled over 300 cycles at 200 mA g−1 with specific capacities stabilizing around 650 mAh g−1 after initial activation.; The 5-cation system achieved a specific capacity of 770 mAh g−1 after 100 cycles following a rate increase to 3 A g−1 for 5 cycles.; Medium entropy oxides (4-cation systems) showed rapid capacity degradation, with the Co-removed variant failing completely after ~10 cycles.; The Coulombic efficiency of the 5-cation TM-HEO stabilized between 99.4% and 99.95% in the range of cycles 60–400.; The 4-cation system without Zn (TM-MEO(-Zn)) exhibited a two-step oxidation process at 1.7 V and 2.2 V, unlike the single-step oxidation of the 5-cation system.; High-loading electrodes (2.3 mg cm−2) maintained Coulombic efficiencies >98.5% and an areal capacity of 1.3 mAh cm−2 after 30 cycles.; No metallic phases or Cu dendrites were detected via TEM/EDX after 100 cycles, despite the conversion reaction mechanism.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the rock-salt structure is preserved as a permanent host matrix during the entire conversion process. While some cations (e.g., Co, Cu) are reduced to metallic states during lithiation, they remain 'trapped' within the defect-rich rock-salt lattice stabilized by unreduced cations (e.g., Mg, Ni). This entropy stabilization lowers the Gibbs free energy, favoring the re-incorporation of reduced cations into the original lattice sites upon delithiation, preventing phase separation and structural collapse.. Limitations: The theoretical capacity cannot be predicted with high accuracy due to unknown additional processes like Zn-Li alloying or intermetallic formation; some 4-cation systems (TM-MEO(-Mg) and TM-MEO(-Ni)) could not be synthesized as single-phase compounds even at high temperatures.. Future work: Further investigations should be pursued to explore the full potential of high entropy oxide electrode materials, including the addition of other cations (Fe, Mn, Cr, V) to develop a modular method for tailoring electrodes to specific needs.. Quote: "The stabilization effect of entropy brings significant benefits for the storage capacity retention of high entropy oxides and greatly improves the cycling stability."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a new spinel high-entropy oxide (Mg0.2Ti0.2Zn0.2Cu0.2Fe0.2)3O4 be used as an anode material for lithium-ion batteries with superior lithium storage properties?. System: Spinel high-entropy oxide (Mg0.2Ti0.2Zn0.2Cu0.2Fe0.2)3O4. Processing: One-step solid state reaction method and subsequent high-energy ball-milling. Test conditions: Current density of 100 mA g−1, 2000 mA g−1; voltage window of 0.01–3.0 V vs. Li/Li+. Findings: Large reversible capacity of 504 mA h g−1 at a current density of 100 mA g−1 after 300 cycles; Exceptional rate capacity of 272 mA h g−1 at 2000 mA g−1; High capacity retention of 96.2% after 800 cycles at 2000 mA g−1. Mechanism: The superior electrochemical performance could be ascribed to the usage of novel (Mg0.2Ti0.2Zn0.2Cu0.2Fe0.2)3O4 particle structure, which can not only buffer the volumetric changes upon lithiation/delithiation processes, but also provide enlarged surface sites for lithium storage and facilitate the charge/electrolyte reaction. Future work: Rational design and use of high-entropy oxides with different electrochemically active elements and novel structure as LIB anode materials might be promising for exploring next-generation energy storage devices. Quote: "delivering a large reversible capacity of 504 mA h g−1 at a current density of 100 mA g−1 after 300 cycles"

card: Paper card. Question: Can the thermodynamic principle of high entropy stabilization be applied to design self-regenerative supported transition metal catalysts that resist sintering through reversible exsolution-dissolution cycles?. System: Cubic high-entropy oxide Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox (Zr:Ni:Fe:Cu:Mn:Co molar ratio 5:1:1:1:1:1) and comparative binary/ternary doped ZrO2 systems (e.g., Zr0.5Cu0.5Ox, Zr0.5(CuMn)0.5Ox). Processing: Mechanochemical synthesis: ZrCl4, NiCl2, FeCl3, CuCl2·2H2O, MnCl2, CoCl2·6H2O, and NaCl were ball-milled for 2 hours total; NaOH was added and milled for 1 hour; calcination in air at 550 °C for 3 hours (heating rate 2 K min−1); followed by washing with water and ethanol and drying at 70 °C. Test conditions: Redox cycling: H2 treatment at 600 °C for 2 h followed by Air treatment at 550 °C; Catalytic testing: CO2 hydrogenation (RWGS) at 400 °C for >500 h continuous operation; Feed gas H2:CO2 = 3:1 at atmospheric pressure. Findings: The high entropy Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox achieved a specific surface area of 84 m2 g−1 due to mild crystallization at 550 °C and mechanochemical particle breakage.; In situ reversible exsolution of CoFeCuNi alloy nanoparticles and reintegration into the ZrO2 matrix were observed over three redox cycles (H2 600 °C + Air 550 °C).; The configurational entropy contribution (TΔSconfig = T × 12.7 J mol−1 K−1) was predominant in the Gibbs free energy (ΔG), driving the stability of the host structure.; During CO2 hydrogenation at 400 °C, the catalyst maintained ~29% CO2 conversion and >90% CO selectivity for over 500 hours without sintering.; Binary doped Zr0.5Cu0.5Ox showed excessive particle growth (average size 37.7 nm) and severe deactivation within 40 hours, unlike the high entropy variant.; Impregnated 5% and 10% NiFeCuCo/ZrOx catalysts suffered severe deactivation within 1–3 hours, whereas the high entropy oxide lasted >500 hours.; XPS analysis confirmed the formation of metallic Co0, Ni0, Cu0, and Fe0 species during H2 reduction, while Mn remained largely as MnO.. Mechanism: The high configurational entropy lowers the Gibbs free energy of the solid solution, stabilizing the host matrix against sintering. During reduction, transition metals exsolve to form active alloy nanoparticles; during oxidation, the entropy-added motivation drives the reintegration of these metals back into the parent oxide lattice, creating a self-regenerative cycle that confines metal species and prevents agglomeration.. Limitations: The study notes that binary and ternary doped ZrO2 samples formed impure phases or showed excessive particle growth, indicating that the high entropy effect is critical for the observed stability; the authors also mention that the exsolved CoFeCuNi NPs could not be described as high entropy alloys themselves.. Future work: The authors propose that the current theory may inspire the design of more supported transition metal catalysts (STMCs) with excellent sintering-resistance performance and suggest that considering entropic contributions is just the beginning for developing unique materials for heterogeneous catalysis.. Quote: "entropy driving force could promote the self-regeneration process is proposed"

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy solid solutions be formed in non-oxide ceramic metal diborides with a hexagonal layered structure, and do they exhibit superior hardness and oxidation resistance compared to their constituent individual diborides?. System: Seven equimolar five-component metal diborides: (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Mo0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Mo0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Cr0.2Ti0.2)B2, and (Hf0.2Zr0.2W0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2. Processing: High-energy ball milling (HEBM) for 6 hours in WC media with 60-minute milling/5-minute cooling cycles, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under 30 MPa pressure in vacuum (10^-2 Torr). Test conditions: Hardness measured via Vickers indentation at 200 kgf/mm2 with 15s hold time; oxidation resistance assessed via sequential isothermal annealing in flowing dry air at 800–1500 °C for 1 hour per step. Findings: Six of the seven compositions formed a single-phase hexagonal AlB2 structure with greater than 92% of theoretical density.; Aberration-corrected STEM confirmed 2-D high-entropy metal layers separated by rigid boron nets with no detectable layered segregation along the c-axis.; The measured standard deviations of lattice spacings between basal (0001) planes were only ~0.6% of the average c lattice parameter.; Hardness of the high-entropy diborides was generally greater than the average hardness of the five individual constituent metal diborides.; Oxidation resistance was generally better than the average of individual components, with HEB#1 and HEB#7 maintaining shape at 1500 °C while TiB2 pulverized.; Revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factors based on lattice constants (δc) of 3.9% to 5.2% rationalized single-phase formation, whereas the non-single-phase specimen had δc ≈ 6.2%.; Minor secondary oxide phases ((Zr, Hf)O2) were observed in six specimens, and a secondary (Ti1.6W2.4)B4 phase was found in the W-containing specimen.. Mechanism: The formation of high-entropy solid solutions is rationalized by a revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factor calculated from lattice constants rather than atomic radii; the rigid 2-D boron net constrains the metal layers, reducing the effective size mismatch (δa) and allowing entropy stabilization of the disordered solid solution despite larger atomic size differences in the c-direction.. Limitations: The presence of porosity and oxide inclusions resulting from the HEBM procedure adversely affected hardness and oxidation resistance; MoB2 is metastable at room temperature and W2B5 starting powder has limited solubility; the study did not fully optimize microstructure for maximum property performance.. Future work: Further systematic investigation of hardness, oxidation resistance, and other properties is needed, particularly focusing on processing optimization to achieve fully-dense and oxide-free specimens and utilizing the large compositional design space to tailor protective oxide scales.. Quote: "Greater than 92% of the theoretical densities have been generally achieved with largely uniform compositions from nanoscale to microscale."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the origin of the CO oxidation activity of Ruthenium nanoparticles (Ru NPs)?. System: Ruthenium nanoparticles (Ru NPs) with face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures. Processing: Chemical reduction methods using Ru(acac)3 and RuCl3 · nH2O as metal precursors, and poly(N-vinyl-2-pyrrolidone) (PVP) as the stabilizing agent. Test conditions: High-energy X-ray diffraction experiments at beamline BL04B2 at SPring-8 in Japan, using X-rays of energy 61.46 keV. Findings: The CO oxidation activity of fcc Ru NPs increases with increasing particle size, despite the decrease in surface area; The lattice parameter of fcc Ru NPs is larger than the theoretical value of fcc Ru bulk and tends to increase with decreasing particle size; The lattice distortion of fcc Ru NPs is nearly independent of particle size, while the lattice distortion of hcp Ru NPs decreases with increasing particle size; The B factor, related to static atomic displacement, increases slightly with particle size for both fcc and hcp Ru NPs; The catalytic activity of fcc Ru NPs is higher than that of hcp Ru NPs for particle sizes larger than 3.5 nm; The lattice distortion and B factor are more correlated to the CO oxidation activity than the domain surface area; For small particles with sizes below 3.5 nm, lattice distortions of the close-packed plane in the hcp Ru NPs are greater than those in the fcc Ru NPs. Mechanism: The enhancement of the CO oxidation activity in fcc Ru NPs may be caused by an increase in imperfections due to lattice distortions of close-packed planes and static atomic displacements. Limitations: The study did not assess the direct relation between the structural characterization and CO oxidation activity, as the measurements were performed in a non-reactive gaseous environment. Quote: "Enhancement of the CO oxidation activity in fcc Ru NPs may be caused by an increase in imperfections due to lattice distortions of close-packed planes and static atomic displacements"

card: Paper card. Question: Why does the Mn-free HEA (CrFeCoNi) exhibit higher ballistic resistance than the Mn-containing Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi), and what are the underlying deformation mechanisms during high-speed impact?. System: CrMnFeCoNi (Cantor alloy) and CrFeCoNi (Mn-free companion). Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with 2NN MEAM potential; ballistic impact simulated by a 3 nm iron rigid sphere at 25 nm/ps; uniaxial tension at strain rates of 5 × 10^7, 5 × 10^8, and 5 × 10^9 s^-1; temperatures of 70 K, 300 K, and 1000 K.. Test conditions: Room temperature (300 K) for ballistic impact; high strain rates (10^7 to 10^9 s^-1); plate thicknesses of 2.29 nm and 6.04 nm; bullet speed 25 nm/ps.. Findings: The Mn-free HEA (CrFeCoNi) blocked the high-speed sphere at a smaller penetration depth (2 ps) compared to the Mn-containing HEA (2.5 ps).; The Mn-free HEA exhibited stronger interatomic bonding with a cohesive energy of -4.25 eV per atom, versus -4.01 eV per atom for the Mn-containing alloy.; Higher strain rates induced more active dislocations, significantly enhancing the strain hardening and toughness of the Mn-free HEA.; Dislocation tangling occurred earlier and more easily in the Mn-containing HEA due to Mn's larger atomic radius causing lattice distortion.; The Mn-containing HEA showed more amorphization and structural damage throughout the plate, while the Mn-free HEA maintained better structural integrity.; Deformation twinning was not a dominant factor at room temperature; planar-slip dislocations played the predominant role in plastic deformation.; The Mn-free HEA had a lower stacking fault energy (more negative) than the Mn-containing HEA, favoring the dissociation of full dislocations into partial dislocations.. Mechanism: The superior ballistic resistance of CrFeCoNi is attributed to its stronger interatomic bonding (due to Mn's lower electron work function in CrMnFeCoNi) and higher dislocation density generated at high strain rates. In CrFeCoNi, energy is absorbed by activating dislocations and strain hardening, whereas in CrMnFeCoNi, weaker bonding and easier dislocation tangling lead to bond breaking, amorphization, and severe structural damage.. Limitations: The MD simulation dimensions (nanometers) are significantly smaller than real-world ballistic tests (millimeters to centimeters), which may limit the space for dislocation development, though the authors argue this does not affect the calculated influence of Mn on bonding strength.. Future work: Sufficient attention needs to be given to the modification of the atomic bonding strength in addition to the plastic deformation mechanism when designing armor and energy-absorption HEAs and related materials.. Quote: "Stronger atomic bonding and higher dislocation densities make the CrFeCoNi easier to be strain hardened with elevated toughness to resist high-speed deformation"

W2093974253.title: Tensile properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys

card: Paper card. Question: What are the atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the exceptional damage tolerance (high strength, ductility, and fracture toughness) of the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase fcc solid solution). Processing: Arc-melting high-purity elemental starting materials, drop casting into copper moulds, cold forging and cross rolling at room temperature, recrystallization at 800 °C (grain size ∼6 μm), followed by ion milling (5 kV) or twin jet polishing (10 °C, 13 mA/12 V) to create electron-transparent foils with cracks. Test conditions: In situ straining in an aberration-corrected TEM (FEI Tecnai G2 F20, 200 kV) at room temperature using pulsed tensile loading (axial displacement rate ∼1.0 μm s⁻¹). Findings: Early deformation is dominated by the easy motion of Shockley partial dislocations (1/6<112> type) and the continuous nucleation/annihilation of stacking faults (SFs).; Interactions between partials on different {111} planes form stable 'stacking-fault parallelepipeds' (volume defects) that act as formidable obstacles for dislocation motion.; Perfect (undissociated, 1/2<110> type) dislocations move with extreme difficulty in localized bands of planar slip, creating strong barriers that arrest fast-moving partial dislocations.; The motion of perfect dislocations requires overcoming continuous activation barriers, indicative of high friction stress in the alloy.; Nanoscale voids form in the 'semi-cohesive zone' at the intersection of two {111} slip planes, creating fiber-like bridges spanning the crack faces.; These nanobridges (size <200 nm, some ∼100 nm) deform primarily via nano-twinning ({111} twin structure), which accommodates strain and shields the crack tip.; The synergy of these mechanisms yields tensile strength ∼1 GPa, ductility ∼60–70%, and fracture toughness K_JIc > 200 MPa√m.. Mechanism: The authors propose a synergistic sequence where intrinsic toughening arises from easy partial dislocation motion (ductility) followed by strain hardening via stacking-fault parallelepipeds and planar slip bands (strength). Extrinsic toughening occurs via nanoscale twinned bridges that form behind the crack tip, carrying load and shielding the crack tip from the applied driving force.. Limitations: The study notes that 'ultrahigh-resolution observations have to be made at the nanoscale to permit any characterization of mechanisms so close to the crack tip,' and that 'thin foil samples must be used which, under load, cannot display the full constraint of a bulk sample.'. Future work: The authors state that 'further optimization of these mechanisms may present new directions for the future design of advanced metallic materials with unprecedented damage tolerance.'. Quote: "We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility"

Question: Can a hierarchical architecture involving secondary nanoprecipitates form inside primary nanoprecipitates in high-entropy alloys, and can an ultrahigh strength be achieved through a high density of such intragranular hierarchical nanoprecipitates?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (atomic %). Processing: Mechanical alloying (MA) for 49 hours (45h dry + 4h wet with ethanol) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1000°C, 30 MPa pressure, 90°C/min heating rate, and <8 Pa vacuum.. Test conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tension using in situ SEM microtensile testing with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM compression tests at room temperature with an axial displacement rate of 3 nm s–1.. Findings: Tensile yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1.86 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of ~2.52 GPa at room temperature.; Failure strain of ~5.2% achieved alongside the ultrahigh strength values.; Microstructure consists of a primary fcc phase (~82.3 vol %) and a small amount of bcc phase (~17.7 vol %).; The fcc matrix contains a high density of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates: primary γ′ (L12 structure, ~57 nm avg diameter, ~62 vol % in fcc) and secondary γ* (A1 structure, several nm to tens of nm).; Average spacing between adjacent γ′ nanoprecipitates is ~11 nm.; Dislocations were observed to shear both the primary γ′ and secondary γ* precipitates during in situ TEM compression.; Grain diameters average ~409 nm for the fcc phase and ~227 nm for the bcc phase.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is primarily attributed to precipitation strengthening via the shearing mechanism, where dislocations shear both the primary coherent γ′ precipitates and the secondary coherent γ* precipitates, creating an 'exaggerated precipitation strengthening effect' due to the hierarchical obstacle distribution. Additional contributions come from grain-boundary strengthening (due to submicrometer grains) and load transfer via the hard bcc phase.. Limitations: The chemical composition of the secondary γ* precipitates could not be obtained due to their very small sizes.. Future work: The authors suggest the design strategy provides insight for achieving ultrahigh strength in HEAs or other multicomponent alloys, implying further exploration of hierarchical architectures, though specific future experiments are not explicitly detailed beyond the general validation of the strategy.. Quote: "Here, we report a strategy for the design and fabrication of HEAs that can achieve ultrahigh tensile strengths."

W993612368.title: High strain-rate compressive deformation behavior of the Al0.1CrFeCoNi high entropy alloy

card: Paper card. Question: How do individual deformation mechanisms compete or synergize during plastic deformation in high-entropy alloys at ultralow temperatures, and what is the specific deformation pathway activated?. System: Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 (Cantor alloy), Cr25Fe25Co25Ni25, and Cr33.3Co33.3Ni33.3 (atomic %). Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (>99.9% purity) in Ti-gettered argon, remelted 8 times, drop-cast into Cu molds, homogenized at 1200°C for 24 hours, cold rolled to ~80% reduction, recrystallized at 800°C for 1 hour, and quenched in iced water to achieve ~5 μm grain size; tensile specimens prepared by electrical discharge machining.. Test conditions: In situ neutron diffraction under tensile loading at 15 K, 140 K, and room temperature; strain rate of 2.67 × 10−5 s−1 (0.04 mm/min) in the plastic regime; vacuum ~10−5 kPa.. Findings: At 15 K, the alloy exhibited an extraordinarily high strength of ~2.5 GPa combined with ~62% ductility.; Serrated deformation characterized by sharp load drops began beyond 21% strain, with amplitudes approaching 570 MPa near the ultimate tensile strength.; Stacking fault probability (SFP) developed early at stress > 1075 MPa and increased to 27 × 10−3 before fracture, whereas SFP was almost zero at room temperature.; The deformation pathway at 15 K followed a sequence: dislocation slip (yielding at ~718 MPa) → stacking faults (at ~1075 MPa) → twinning and serrations (at ~1270 MPa).; The (220)//LD diffraction peak disappeared almost entirely toward the end of deformation, indicating significant texture development.; The strain-hardening rate at 15 K was stable until fracture, unlike at 295 K where it decreased with deformation.; Fracture occurred via two shear bands at ~90° angles with no significant necking, despite 62% true strain.. Mechanism: The extreme work hardening and large ductility result from the cooperation of multiple deformation mechanisms: dislocation slip initiates deformation, followed by stacking faults and twinning which create additional boundaries that impede dislocation propagation. Stacking faults act as a critical bridge preventing a direct transition to serration-induced failure. The low stacking fault energy and the stability of the face-centered cubic structure at ultralow temperatures, enabled by high-entropy alloying, facilitate this pathway. Local disorder from the multicomponent nature prevents the propagation of serration flow, allowing continued strengthening until major shear bands form.. Limitations: The thermocouples were located at the sample grips rather than on the sample gauge section, meaning there could be a delay in temperature sensing and the local temperature rise in the deformed region could be much higher than measured.. Future work: The authors suggest that insights from in situ experiments point to the role of entropy in the design of structural materials with superior properties, specifically utilizing the unique combination of complex chemistry and simple crystal structure to deploy competitive mechanisms in synergy.. Quote: "The coexistence of multiple deformation pathways raises an important question regarding how individual deformation mechanisms compete or synergize during plastic deformation."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy effects be utilized to induce a significant glass-to-glass transition in metallic glasses, and what are the structural and thermodynamic mechanisms behind this phenomenon?. System: Equiatomic NbNiZrTiCo high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG), with comparative systems NbNiZrTiCu and NbNiZrTiCoCu. Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (Nb, Ni, Zr, Ti, Co, Cu; purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) under high-purity argon, followed by remelting five times; ribbon production via melt-spinning at a wheel surface velocity of 32 m s−1; heat treatment by heating to 855 K (TA) at 20 K min−1 and cooling at 20 K min−1. Test conditions: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at heating rates of 10–50 K min−1 and Flash DSC at >1000 K s−1; in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction from 305 K to 803 K at 30 K min−1; nanoindentation; dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA); atom probe tomography (APT) at 65 K; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) at 200 kV. Findings: The as-prepared NbNiZrTiCo HEMG exhibits an enormous exothermic peak at 781 K with a heat release of 1.65 kJ mol−1, which is approximately 130% of the subsequent crystallization exotherm (1.27 kJ mol−1).; The glass-to-glass transition is irreversible; the heat-treated sample shows a distinct glass transition temperature (Tg) at ~764 K and lacks the first exothermic peak observed in the as-prepared state.; Nanoindentation measurements reveal a drastic increase in hardness from 6.78 GPa to 9.46 GPa (approximately 40% increase) after the transition.; In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction shows a significant non-linear shift of the first peak in the total structure function S(Q) and a narrowing of the full width at half maximum (FWHM) during the transition.; Pair-distribution function (G(r)) analysis indicates a contraction of short-range atomic distances (r11 and r12 shift to low-r) and prominent splitting of the second peak, signifying enhanced short- and medium-range ordering.; Atom probe tomography confirms a uniform element distribution at the sub-nanometer scale in both as-prepared and heat-treated samples, excluding spinodal decomposition.; The calculated lower limit of entropy change (ΔSH−L) for the transition is −1.96 J mol−1 K−1, with a corresponding enthalpy change (ΔHH−L) of −1.65 kJ mol−1.; Substituting Co with Cu to form NbNiZrTiCu (maintaining high excess configurational entropy) and adding Cu to form NbNiZrTiCoCu both result in similar glass-to-glass transitions.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the high configurational entropy (SC) and high excess configurational entropy (SE) dynamically stabilize a high-energy glass state during rapid vitrification by hindering atomic reconstruction and slowing diffusion. Upon heating, this high-energy state undergoes a thermodynamically driven transition to a low-energy, more ordered glass state, releasing a large amount of heat. The transition is driven by the specific combination of high SC and high SE (related to atomic size misfit), which enables the formation of a high-energy glass that is distinct from conventional metallic glasses.. Limitations: The text notes that the observed phase transition is an irreversible process, meaning the calculated entropy change represents a lower limit. Additionally, the detailed structural changes cannot be fully resolved by atom probe tomography due to its limited spatial resolution, and some weak diffraction peaks in crystallized samples could not be identified.. Future work: The authors suggest that the HEMGs may serve as model materials for exploring glass-to-glass transitions and the fundamental nature of glasses in materials science and condensed-matter physics. They also propose potential applications as energetic materials due to the large anomalous exotherm, which could contribute to combustion heats and lower ignition temperatures.. Quote: "An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing configuration entropy affect the energy storage performance and domain structure of lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics, and can it enable a breakthrough in energy density and efficiency?. System: (Bi0.5Na0.5)(Ti1-2xFexNbx)O3 (BNTFN-x, x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 1/3) lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics. Processing: Conventional solid-state reaction method; raw materials mixed by planetary mill for 24 h; calcined at 750–800 °C for 5 h; ball milled with PVB binder at 600 r min−1 for 15 h; pressed into 10 mm pellets at ~300 MPa; sintered at 1050–1250 °C for 2 h with sacrificial powders; polished to ~50–80 μm thickness; silver electrodes fired at 550 °C for 20 min. Test conditions: P-E loops at 10 Hz; frequency-dependent loops from 1 to 200 Hz; cycling up to 10^6 times; charge/discharge tests at 16–24 kV mm−1 and 20–160 °C; Weibull distribution analysis with n=10 samples. Findings: Ultrahigh recoverable energy density (Wrec) of ~13.8 J cm−3 and efficiency (η) of ~82.4% achieved in BNTFN-1/3 (ΔSconfig ~1.79R).; Wrec of BNTFN-1/3 achieved nearly 10 times growth compared to low-entropy BNTFN-0 (0.39 J cm−3).; Breakdown field (Eb) increased from 24 kV mm−1 in BNTFN-0 to 64 kV mm−1 in BNTFN-1/3.; Theoretical Eb of BNTFN-1/3 calculated via Weibull distribution is 64.3 kV mm−1 with a Weibull modulus (β) of 28.1.; Nanodomain size decreased from 100–200 nm in BNTFN-0 to ultrasmall PNRs (2–4 nm) in BNTFN-1/3, below PFM resolution.; Average grain size (Ga) decreased from 3.0 μm (BNTFN-0) to 2.2 μm (BNTFN-1/3) with increasing entropy.; Discharge energy density (WD) of ~2.35 J cm−3 and ultrafast discharge time (t0.9) of ~30.4 ns achieved at 24 kV mm−1.; Energy storage performance remained stable over 10^6 cycles with Wrec ~5.88 ± 0.14 J cm−3 and η ~85.5 ± 0.5%.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the performance enhancement to the enhanced random field and improved breakdown field caused by increasing configuration entropy, which breaks long-range ferroelectric order and decreases nanodomain sizes to ultrasmall polar nanoregions (PNRs). Additionally, the coexistence of in-phase and anti-phase oxygen octahedron tilts creates strong multiple local distortions that delay polarization saturation and increase energy absorption.. Limitations: The text notes that the resolution of PFM was insufficient to effectively identify domain morphology in high-entropy samples, and TEM also could not clearly reveal small-size PNRs, requiring speculation based on HR-TEM Moiré fringes.. Future work: The authors speculate that if the types of elements continue to increase to further improve ΔSconfig, Wrec and η will significantly increase, and they suggest that high-entropy antiferroelectric materials still need to be further designed or attempted.. Quote: "Ultrahigh energy storage density of ~ 13.8 J cm−3 and large efficiency of ~ 82.4% are achieved in high-entropy lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics via high-entropy strategy, realizing nearly ten times growth."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a high-entropy design strategy be utilized to simultaneously achieve ultrahigh recoverable energy storage density (Wrec) and ultrahigh efficiency (η) in lead-free relaxor ferroelectric ceramics?. System: Lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics with the composition [(K0.2Na0.8)0.8Li0.08Ba0.02Bi0.1](Nb0.68Sc0.02Hf0.08Zr0.1Ta0.08Sb0.04)O3 (KNN-H), based on the K0.2Na0.8NbO3 lattice.. Processing: Conventional solid-state reaction method: starting powders were planetary ball-milled for 24 h, dried at 120 °C for 2 h, calcined at 800 °C for 5 h, mixed with 0.5 wt% PVB binder, pressed into pellets at 300 MPa, heated to 550 °C to burn out binder, and sintered at 1230 °C in closed crucibles for 2 h.. Test conditions: Electric fields up to 740 kV cm−1 for P-E loops; temperatures from 25 to 140 °C and frequencies from 1 to 300 Hz for stability tests; cycling up to 10^6 times; charge/discharge tests at 300 kV cm−1.. Findings: A giant recoverable energy storage density (Wrec) of ~10.06 J cm−3 was achieved.; An ultrahigh energy storage efficiency (η) of ~90.8% was realized.; The breakdown electric field (Eb) was enhanced to 740 kV cm−1.; The Vickers hardness (Hv) reached ~7.70 GPa, significantly higher than pure KNN (~3.24 GPa).; The discharge energy density (WD) was ~3.26 J cm−3 with an ultrafast discharge rate (t0.9) of ~34 ns.; The material exhibited temperature-insensitive energy storage (Wrec ~3.38 ± 0.20 J cm−3) from 25 to 140 °C.; The material showed frequency-insensitive properties with Wrec ~4.46 ± 0.25 J cm−3 from 1 to 300 Hz.; Polarization vectors formed polar nanoregions (PNRs) with sizes of ~1–3 nm.. Mechanism: The high-entropy strategy induces 'local polymorphic distortion' characterized by rhombohedral-orthorhombic-tetragonal-cubic (R-O-T-C) multiphase nanoclusters and random oxygen octahedral tilt. This structure creates a strong random field that reduces PNR size, delays polarization saturation, and drives the system back to a nonpolar state (near-zero Pr), resulting in slim P-E loops, high breakdown strength, and high efficiency.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study itself, though it notes that achieving Wrec ≥10 J cm−3 with η ≥90% simultaneously was a previous bottleneck in lead-free ceramics.. Future work: The authors propose that this high-entropy strategy opens an effective avenue to design dielectric materials with ultrahigh comprehensive energy storage performance to meet the demanding requirements of advanced energy storage applications.. Quote: "A giant Wrec ~10.06 J cm−3 is realized in lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics, especially with an ultrahigh η ~90.8%."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the structure, performance, and application of BiFeO3 nanomaterials?. System: BiFeO3 (BFO) and its derivatives. Findings: BFO exhibits both (anti)ferromagnetic and ferroelectric properties at room temperature; BFO has a ferroelectric phase transition Curie temperature (TC) of 1103 K and a G-type antiferromagnetic phase transition Neel temperature (TN) of 643 K; BFO-based nanomaterials have been prepared in various forms, including ceramics, thin films, and nanostructures; The morphology, structures, and properties of BFO can be modified by ion substitution, formation of solid solutions, and epitaxial strain; BFO-based nanomaterials have potential applications in multiferroic devices with novel functions. Mechanism: The ferroelectric polarization of BFO originates from the relative shift of Bi3+ from the oxygen octahedron, which causes the formation of an electric dipole moment. Future work: Further research is needed to develop BFO-based nanomaterials with improved properties and to explore their potential applications. Quote: "Multiferroic nanomaterials have attracted great interest due to simultaneous two or more properties"

Paper card. Question: How do the morphologies and sizes of BFO nanostructures affect their magnetic properties?. System: BiFeO3 (BFO) nanostructures. Findings: 1.62; magnetic response increases dramatically below 62 nm; theoretic values of TC and TN depend on the particle sizes; strain can be used to modify the exchange bias, the magnetic orientation, and giant magnetoresistive response of spin valves. Mechanism: Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction plays a dominant role in low strain, and the increased single-ion anisotropy at high strain results in deviation of the perpendicular relationship between antiferromagnetic axis and the polarization direction. Quote: "the morphologies and sizes largely affect the magnetic properties"

Paper card. Question: How can the photovoltaic effect in BiFeO3 nanomaterials be improved and utilized in photodetector systems?. System: BiFeO3 (BFO) nanomaterials. Test conditions: 450-nm light illumination, heating and cooling states. Findings: An ITO/BFO/Ag self-powered photodetector was designed to investigate potential applications of the BFO photodetector; A photocurrent of about 10 nA was obtained by this photodetector; The pyroelectric effect was able to adjust the Schottky barrier height, which leads to the enhanced photocurrent; The photodetector can be used to detect 450-nm light in real time; Temperature played an important role in improvement of photovoltaic performance; The photovoltaic performance of the BFO photodetector can be modulated by applying different temperatures. Mechanism: The pyroelectric effect was able to adjust the Schottky barrier height, which leads to the enhanced photocurrent. Limitations: The physical mechanisms of photovoltaic effect and photocatalytic behavior in BFO nanomaterials are still elusive. Future work: Further studies are deserved to expound the physical mechanisms of photovoltaic effect and photocatalytic behavior in BFO nanomaterials. Quote: "by using the photovoltaic–pyroelectric coupled effect"

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing the configurational entropy by introducing multiple salts into a liquid electrolyte impact the thermodynamic and kinetic properties, specifically solvation structures, ion transport, and interphase stability, in lithium batteries?. System: 0.6 M High-Entropy (HE) electrolyte composed of 0.15 M LiFSI, 0.15 M LiTFSI, 0.15 M LiDFOB, and 0.15 M LiNO3 in dimethoxyethane (DME) solvent; compared against single-salt electrolytes (0.6 M LiFSI-DME, 0.6 M LiTFSI-DME, 0.6 M LiDFOB-DME) and a 0.36 M LiNO3-DME electrolyte.. Processing: Electrolytes prepared by dissolving specific amounts of lithium salts (LiFSI, LiTFSI, LiDFOB, LiNO3) in DME solvent in an Ar-filled glove box (H2O < 0.1 ppm, O2 < 0.1 ppm) at room temperature; total lithium ion concentration maintained at 0.6 M for the HE electrolyte.. Test conditions: Electrochemical cycling in CR2032 coin cells at room temperature; Li||LiFePO4 cells (2.5–5.0 V) for oxidation stability; Li||NCM811 cells (2.8–4.3 V) for cathode compatibility; Li||Cu cells for plating/stripping efficiency; Li||Li4Ti5O12 cells for rate capability; symmetric Li||Li cells for impedance and transference number; Cryo-TEM at -170 °C; Operando 7Li NMR; Raman spectroscopy at room temperature.. Findings: The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte exhibits a 7Li NMR chemical shift of -0.68 ppm, indicating weaker solvation interaction compared to single-salt electrolytes (e.g., -1.19 ppm for LiTFSI-DME).; The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte shows an oxidation stability limit up to ~4.51 V, higher than the 4.36 V limit of the 0.6 M LiFSI-DME control.; Lithium plating/stripping in the 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte achieves a Coulombic efficiency of up to 98.6%, considerably higher than the 0.6 M LiFSI-DME electrolyte.; The 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte has a lithium-ion transference number of 0.46 and ionic conductivity of ~12.1 mS cm−1, compared to 0.39 and 9.6 mS cm−1 for the LiFSI-DME electrolyte.; At a rate of 5.0 C, the 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte retains ~115 mAh g−1 capacity in Li||Li4Ti5O12 cells, whereas the LiFSI-DME electrolyte retains only ~40 mAh g−1.; Li||NCM811 cells with 0.6 M HE-DME electrolyte achieve over 82% capacity retention after 100 cycles at 0.333 C charged to 4.3 V.; Long-term cycling at 6.0 C in Li||NCM811 cells shows ~85% capacity retention after 500 cycles and ~80% after 600 cycles.; Cryo-TEM reveals a thin (~6 nm) inorganic-rich SEI in the HE-DME electrolyte, contrasting with a thicker, non-uniform, solvent-decomposition-dominated SEI in the LiFSI-DME electrolyte.. Mechanism: The introduction of multiple salts creates a diversity of anionic groups that participate in solvation structures, resulting in a larger variety of lithium-ion solvation environments (over 30 types predicted by DFT). This entropy-dominated diversity weakens the solvation strength between lithium ions and solvents/anions, facilitating lithium-ion diffusivity and charge transfer. The weaker solvation and diverse anion participation lead to the formation of inorganic-rich, stable interphase layers (SEI/CEI) that suppress solvent decomposition and dendrite growth.. Limitations: The text notes that the DME solvent has relatively low oxidation stability, which is a challenge for high-voltage cathodes, although the HE electrolyte mitigates this. The study focuses on a specific four-salt prototype, and the compositional landscape is described as huge and largely unexplored.. Future work: The authors propose that the compositional landscape of HE materials is huge and suggest that raising entropy by introducing multiple salts can be used to improve functional properties, where the choice of specific salts and solvents should be guided by their interactions with specific anode and cathode chemistry. They also mention preparing a five-component salt HE electrolyte to support even longer stable cycling.. Quote: "Unlike all liquid electrolytes so far reported, the participation of several anionic groups in this electrolyte induces a larger diversity in solvation structures, unexpectedly decreasing solvation strengths between lithium ions and solvents/anions."

Paper card. Question: How do single and high-entropy (HE) electrolyte systems with different lithium salts and concentrations behave at the molecular level?. System: High entropy liquid electrolytes with different lithium salts in dimethoxyethane (DME) solvent; specific ratio of 1:10 salt/solvent. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with OPLS-AA force field; system packing via Packmol (60 × 60 × 60 Å box, 1200 DME + 120 salt molecules); energy minimization via conjugate-gradient; isothermal-isobaric ensemble at 300 K for 5 ns; canonical ensemble equilibration for 6 ns followed by 10 ns production run with 0.5 fs time-step; DFT calculations using Gaussian 09 with B3LYP/6-31 + G(d,p) for geometry and B3LYP/6-311 + +G(3df,3dp) for energy. Test conditions: 300 K (room temperature); cut-off distance of 1.1 nm for Lennard-Jones interactions; snapshots obtained every 0.5 ps. Findings: Simulation boxes were randomly packed with 1200 molecules of DME and 120 salt molecules to achieve a 1:10 salt/solvent ratio; Isothermal-isobaric ensemble simulations at 300 K were performed for 5 ns to obtain correct volumes; Canonical ensemble simulations were continued for another 10 ns after equilibration; Radial density functions and diffusivities of lithium ions were computed using the MDAnalysis package; Solvation structures were analyzed using the Python Materials Genomics (pymatgen) package; Partial charges were computed using Møller–Plesset second-order perturbation method with cc-pVTZ(-f) basis set. Quote: "Molecules and ions were described by the optimized potentials for a liquid simulations all-atom (OPLS-AA) force field."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy transition-metal carbides be designed to exhibit tunable plasmonic properties in the near-IR to visible range while maintaining high thermal stability and mechanical hardness?. System: High-entropy transition-metal carbides (PHECs), specifically the archetype HfTa4C5 and a set of 14 six-element alloys (Carbon + 5 transition metals from groups 4, 5, and 6: Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W). Processing: Computational: High-throughput disorder modeling using the Partial Occupation (POCC) method within the AFLOW framework to generate Boltzmann ensembles of superlattices, followed by time-dependent density-functional perturbation theory (TD-DFPT) calculations using VASP and turboEELS. Experimental: Ball-milling of TaC and HfC powders (4:1 ratio) followed by Field Assisted Sintering Technology (FAST) at 2100–2400 °C, 40–55 MPa, and 30–40 min hold times.. Test conditions: Computational: Optical limit (q=0) and varying transferred momentum (q); temperatures up to 1500 K. Experimental: Electron-energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) on HfTa4C5 cross-sections at beam energy 300 keV, with temperatures ranging from room temperature (~25 °C) to 1200 °C.. Findings: HfTa4C5 exhibits a crossover energy (E0) at 2.41 eV (simulated) and 2.7 eV (experimental), marking a metal-to-dielectric transition in the visible range.; The plasmonic response of PHECs can be tuned from the near-IR to visible by varying the transition metal components and their concentration.; Systems 3-HfNbTaTiZrC5 and 14-HfNbTaTiWC5 show the highest effective EELS intensity (h) and lowest energy loss dissipation, indicating good plasmonic properties.; The crossover energy E0 spans a wide range from near-IR to visible, increasing monotonically with the atomic number of constituents within each group.; The screened plasmon resonance in HfTa4C5 remains clearly recognizable up to 1500 K, demonstrating stability far above the melting points of standard plasmonic metals like Ag and Au.; Substitution of Hf with 3d metals (V, Cr) leads to plasmonic resonance deterioration, while group 6 metals (W, Mo) cause broadening of the EELS peak.; The presence of Ta is necessary but not sufficient for obtaining good plasmonic PHECs; the best results come from combining high-Z elements from groups 4 and 5 (Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta).. Mechanism: The plasmonic response arises from a balance between intraband transitions (Drude-like, negative contribution to real dielectric function) and interband transitions (positive contribution). The crossover energy E0 corresponds to the energy where the real part of the dielectric function switches sign, determined by the energy difference (δ) between the Fermi level and the edge of the interband transition band (b2). Higher atomic number elements shift the Fermi level deeper into the d-band, increasing δ and causing a blue-shift in E0.. Limitations: The study does not include time evolution or de-excitation processes of plasmons, which are affected by electron-phonon scattering. Experimental characterization beyond 1500 K is noted as arduous due to equipment limitations. Some systems exhibit high dissipation where peaks cannot be associated with collective plasmon-like oscillations.. Future work: The authors propose using the discovered rules to design tailored high-entropy ceramics with optical properties optimized for specific applications, such as exploiting dissipative systems for photothermal applications or using quasi-neutral elements (Ti, W) to stabilize PHECs while altering mechanical/thermal properties.. Quote: "We chose high-entropy transition-metal carbides because of their exceptional thermal, chemical stability, and mechanical properties."

card: Paper card. Question: Can an entropy-forming-ability (EFA) descriptor based on first-principles energy distribution spectra predict the synthesizability of disordered five-metal refractory carbides as homogeneous high-entropy single phases?. System: Five-metal refractory carbides (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5, HfMoTaWZrC5, HfMoTiWZrC5, HfMoVWZrC5) derived from eight metals (Hf, Nb, Mo, Ta, Ti, V, W, Zr) and carbon. Processing: Solid-state synthesis via ball milling (2 h total, 30-min intervals with 10-min rests) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2200 °C, 100 °C/min heating rate, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 5-min dwell in vacuum/argon atmosphere. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification; Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for chemical homogeneity; Nanoindentation at 27 °C ± 0.5 °C with 50 mN load for Vickers hardness (HV) and elastic modulus (E); Williamson–Hall analysis for lattice strain. Findings: The EFA descriptor correctly predicted that MoNbTaVWC5 (EFA = 125 (eV/atom)−1), HfNbTaTiZrC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1), and HfNbTaTiVC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1) would form homogeneous single phases, while HfMoVWZrC5 (EFA = 37 (eV/atom)−1) would not.; Six of the nine synthesized compositions (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5) exhibited single rock-salt fcc phases, whereas the three lowest-EFA compositions showed multiple secondary phases.; Vickers hardness of HfNbTaTiZrC5 reached 32 GPa, which is 50% higher than the rule of mixtures (ROM) prediction, and HfTaTiWZrC5 reached 33 GPa.; The Pearson correlation between the inverse EFA (EFA−1) and lattice distortion (ε) was 0.97, and the Spearman rank correlation was 0.98, validating EFA as a synthesizability descriptor.; Lattice distortion (ε) ranged from 0.063% for MoNbTaVWC5 (most homogeneous) to 0.325% for HfMoVWZrC5 (least homogeneous).; The highest-EFA composition MoNbTaVWC5 formed a homogeneous phase despite using precursors Mo2C and W2C with different structures (orthorhombic and hexagonal) and stoichiometries compared to the rock-salt product.; Vibrational contributions to formation free energy at 2000 K ranged from ~0 meV/atom to −31 meV/atom, which are significantly smaller than the configurational entropy contributions required to overcome formation enthalpy barriers (50–150 meV/atom).; A threshold of EFA ~50 (eV/atom)−1 was identified as the point above which homogeneous disordered single phases are likely to form.. Mechanism: The authors argue that a narrow energy distribution spectrum (low standard deviation σ) implies a low energy cost to access metastable configurations, promoting configurational randomness (entropy) at finite temperatures. This entropy stabilization allows the disordered rock-salt phase to remain locked in upon cooling, even when competing ordered phases exist. Enhanced hardness is attributed to mass disorder causing impedance mismatch that scatters dislocations, increasing resistance to plastic deformation.. Limitations: The study notes that the Williamson–Hall formalism does not provide particularly accurate absolute values of lattice strain (ε), though it is effective for relative comparisons. Additionally, the vibrational contribution to entropy is an order of magnitude smaller than configurational entropy, and the study did not investigate the specific effect of carbon stoichiometry on melting points.. Future work: The authors state that an investigation of the effect of carbon stoichiometry is clearly warranted to understand how vacancies might further improve high-temperature performance, although it is outside the scope of this study.. Quote: "The descriptor correctly predicts the ease with which compositions can be experimentally synthesized as rock-salt high-entropy homogeneous phases, validating the ansatz, and in some cases, going beyond intuition."

card: Paper card. Question: How can an all-dielectric metasurface simultaneously achieve high brightness, large color gamut, narrow reflection bandwidth, and diffraction-limit resolution to meet commercial requirements for structural color?. System: Silicon (Si) nanodisks on a sapphire substrate, combined with a refractive index matching layer (dimethyl sulfoxide, DMSO, n=1.48 or PMMA). Processing: Fabrication on commercially available silicon-on-sapphire (SOS) wafers using electron-beam lithography with PMMA resist, lift-off to create a Cr mask, and reactive ion etching (RIE) in an Oxford Plasma System; optical characterization via bright-field microscopy and spectrometry. Test conditions: Bright-field optical microscopy (×50 objective, NA=0.55 for spectra; ×100 objective, NA=0.9 for resolution), white light illumination, samples tested in air and infiltrated with DMSO (n=1.48) or packaged with PMMA. Findings: The experimentally demonstrated color gamut increased from 78% of sRGB in air to 181.8% of sRGB, 135.6% of Adobe RGB, and 97.2% of Rec.2020 when infiltrated with DMSO.; The full width at half maximum (FWHM) of reflection peaks narrowed to 34–40 nm in DMSO, which is 40% narrower than in air.; Background reflection from the substrate was suppressed to approximately zero when the refractive index matching layer was applied.; High reflectance was preserved at ~74% for magnetic dipole resonance across the visible spectrum with the matching layer.; Spatial resolution reached the diffraction limit with pixel sizes as small as 2 × 2 arrays of nanodisks (center-to-center distances down to 190 nm).; The color impression remained uniform and distinguishable even when pixel sizes were reduced from 5 × 5 to 2 × 2 arrays.; The roughness of the fabricated nanostructures was measured to be smaller than 10 nm with sidewalls nearly 90° in the vertical direction.; Single-crystalline Si provided a gamut area 110% and 238% larger than poly-crystalline and amorphous Si, respectively.. Mechanism: The refractive index matching layer reduces the refractive index contrast between the sapphire substrate and the environment, suppressing background reflection. Additionally, the layer pushes the electric dipole resonance closer to the magnetic dipole resonance, creating destructive interference (Kerker condition) that narrows the reflection bandwidth (FWHM) and enhances color purity.. Limitations: The text notes that previous hybrid nanostructures suffered from incompatible fabrication technologies and deformation of top layers during etching, but states that the current single-crystalline Si approach overcomes these specific limitations; no explicit limitations of the current study are stated beyond the general need for commercialization.. Future work: The authors propose that this research routes a key step towards the commercialization of structural color in dynamic displays, optical security, and information storage.. Quote: "Consequently, the experimentally demonstrated gamut has been increased to around 181.8% of sRGB, 135.6% of Adobe RGB, and 97.2% of Rec.2020."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the role of vibrational contributions in the thermodynamic stability of high-entropy carbides, and under what conditions should they be included in stability predictions?. System: (HfNbTaTiV)C, (HfNbTaTiW)C, and (HfNbTaTiZr)C (referred to as HEC-V, HEC-W, and HEC-Zr). Processing: Computational integration of the Partial Occupation (POCC) algorithm with the AFLOW Automatic Phonon Library (APL); structures relaxed until forces were below 10−3 eV/ℓ; phonon calculations used a displacement magnitude of 0.015 ℓ in supercells with at least 180 atoms; TPOCC set to 2473 K.. Test conditions: Harmonic approximation at temperatures ranging from 0 K to synthesis temperatures; comparison against binary carbide precursors (rock-salt phases) and decomposition products; Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) used for comparison.. Findings: Vibrational contributions shift the transition temperature for HEC-W by approximately 150 K, whereas they have only a small effect on HEC-V and HEC-Zr.; Mass disorder on the cation sublattice destabilizes the high-entropy carbides (increases vibrational free energy), while force constant disorder has a stabilizing effect.; The vibrational entropy change (ΔSvib) for HEC-W is 0.22 kB/atom, which is an order of magnitude larger than the 0.04 kB/atom observed for HEC-V and HEC-Zr.; The Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) incorrectly predicts HEC-V to be more strongly stabilized by vibrations than HEC-W, failing to capture phonon anomalies present in VC.; Vibrational contributions shift the decomposition phase transition temperatures for HEC-V and HEC-W to lower temperatures by 80 K and 160 K, respectively.; The carbide sublattice distorts to accommodate different metal cations, resulting in nearest-neighbor metal-carbon distances that are closer to the average of binary carbides to maximize configurational entropy.; Vibrations alone are insufficient to stabilize HEC-V against decomposition at 2000 K, as the vibrational free energy change is smaller than the distance to the convex hull.. Mechanism: The authors argue that vibrational contributions are significant when precursors or decomposition products have different nearest-neighbor environments or symmetries compared to the high-entropy carbide. Specifically, the lower symmetry of hexagonal WC compared to the rock-salt HEC-W leads to depressed vibrational entropy in the precursor, creating a large stabilization gain upon forming the disordered phase. Conversely, when precursors and the HEC share similar atomic environments (as in HEC-V and HEC-Zr), the vibrational entropy changes are minimal.. Limitations: The study relies on the harmonic approximation, ignoring anharmonic effects which become significant at high temperatures and could stabilize structures with imaginary frequencies; the calculations use the PBE functional which may affect phonon frequencies; the ideal high-temperature configurational entropy is used, which overestimates entropic contributions at lower temperatures; and the study is limited to stoichiometric samples without accounting for vacancies or interstitial carbon.. Future work: The authors suggest that anharmonic contributions should be included to improve accuracy, that the effect of the exchange-correlation functional (e.g., SCAN vs. PBE) on transition temperatures needs investigation, and that defects such as vacancies and interstitial carbon atoms should be explored in future research on high-entropy ceramics.. Quote: "The contribution of vibrations to the stability of high-entropy ceramics is still controversial."

Paper card. Question: How to generate and validate derivative structures for (HfNbTaTi)RC high-entropy carbides to ensure converged vibrational free energy calculations.. System: (HfNbTaTi)RC where R = V, W, Zr. Processing: Created 49 ordered representative structures using the AFLOW-POCC algorithm from a rock-salt parent structure (space group: Fm-3m, #225); KPPRA value increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K converged within 1 meV/atom; APL supercells generated using standard conventional representations; relaxation and static calculations performed with exact same k-point densities.. Test conditions: Vibrational free energy convergence target of 1 meV/atom at 300 K; k-point densities required to be identical for relaxation and static calculations to avoid residual force increases.. Findings: 49 ordered representative structures were created for the (HfNbTaTi)RC system.; KPPRA values were increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K was converged within 1 meV/atom.; Using different k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations leads to an increase in residual forces by up to two orders of magnitude.; This residual force increase was observed even at KPPRA values above 20,000.; Standard conventional representations were used to generate APL supercells to achieve a more spherical shape.. Mechanism: The authors argue that maintaining exact same k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations is critical to prevent large residual forces, which can occur even at high KPPRA values if densities differ.. Quote: "producing 49 ordered representative structures."

card: Paper card. Question: How can short-range order (SRO) be detected in medium/high-entropy alloys (MEAs/HEAs) using non-imaging and imaging techniques, and what is the impact of SRO on their physical and mechanical properties?. System: NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA), CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNiPd high-entropy alloys (HEAs), VNiCo MEA, Ru-based HEA nanoparticles (NPs), and a 15-element HEA (15-HEA). Processing: Synthesis of NiCoCr samples followed by two heat treatments: water-quenching after homogenization at 1,200°C, and aging at 1,000°C for 120 h followed by slow furnace cooling; synthesis of VNiCo MEA; synthesis of Ru-based HEA NPs via carbothermal shock; irradiation of NiCoCr with Ni ions at doses up to 0.3 displacements per atoms (dpa). Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD), neutron diffraction, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS/EXAFS), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), geometric phase analysis (GPA), nano-indentation, bulk tensile tests, and irradiation tests. Findings: In NiCoCr MEA, EXAFS fitting revealed that Cr atoms favored bonding with Ni and Co atoms, while Cr-Cr bonds were disfavored, indicated by a larger Debye-Waller (DW) factor for Cr-Cr bonds compared to Cr-Ni and Cr-Co bonds.; Aging NiCoCr MEA at 1,000°C for 120 h followed by slow cooling resulted in superlattice streaking in diffraction patterns and contrast in dark-field images, indicating increased SRO compared to water-quenched samples.; In VNiCo MEA, EDS mapping showed an alternating pattern of V-enriched regions sandwiching Co- or Ni-enriched regions, with a spacing of less than 1 nm, confirming SRO.; Irradiation of NiCoCr MEA to 0.3 dpa decreased Ni-Cr bond distances from 2.51 Å to 2.49 Å and reduced DW factors from 0.002 Å² to 0.001 Å², suggesting radiation increases the amount of SRO.; The aged NiCoCr MEA showed a 25% increase in yield point compared to the water-quenched sample, confirming the strengthening effect of SRO.; The stacking fault energy (SFE) for the aged NiCoCr sample was double that of the water-quenched sample, indicating a positive correlation between SRO degree and SFE.; In VNiCo MEA, SRO-dislocation coupling was observed, where dislocations were sluggish through SRO domains, leading to increased strain hardening during tensile deformation.; APT analysis of annealed NiCoCr MEA showed peak intensity variations spanning approximately 2 nm, classified as local chemical ordering (LCO) rather than typical SRO.. Mechanism: SRO arises from preferential bonding between specific elements (e.g., Cr-Ni/Co in NiCoCr, V-Co/Ni in VNiCo), leading to local lattice distortions and alternating chemical planes. These distortions create energetically favorable domains that impede dislocation motion (SRO-dislocation coupling), increasing yield strength and strain hardening. Radiation exposure can enhance SRO by altering bond distances and reducing lattice disorder.. Limitations: XRD and neutron diffraction total scattering measurements were not able to identify evidence of ordering in NiCoCr MEA because PDF analysis could not distinguish bond lengths and vibrations of pairs of atoms with comparable atomic sizes. TEM imaging alone could not determine the exact bonding preferences causing alternating contrast; element-specific methods were required. Most studies focused on MEAs with 3d transition metals, limiting understanding of more complex HEAs with 4d or 5d metals.. Future work: Conduct studies on HEA samples containing higher numbers of elements and combinations of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals to uncover how SRO arises in a wider compositional space. Prepare samples with varying degrees of SRO through controlled heat treatments to accurately assess the impact of SRO on mechanical properties. Investigate the impact of SRO on the catalytic properties of HEA nanoparticles. Develop new non-imaging and imaging techniques, such as 4D-STEM and atom probe tomography (APT), to better characterize SRO.. Quote: "Cr atoms favored bonding with Ni and Co atoms, and disfavored forming bonds with other Cr atoms."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the miscibility gap in bimetallic Co-Mo alloys be overcome to create tunable, highly active catalysts for ammonia decomposition using earth-abundant elements?. System: Quinary CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 where x + y = 70) and control samples of bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru. Processing: Carbothermal shock technique involving flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon nanofibers; temperature reached 2000–2300 K with ramping rates on the order of 10^5 K s−1 and shock duration of ~55 ms. Test conditions: Ammonia decomposition in a plug flow reactor at 250–600 °C using 5 vol% NH3 (and 100 vol% NH3 for specific tests) at a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 36 L gcat−1 h−1. Findings: HEA-Co25Mo45 achieved a mass-specific reaction rate of 22.1 gNH3 gmetals−1 h−1 at 500 °C, representing an improvement factor of ~19 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~3 versus Ru.; The most active catalyst, HEA-Co25Mo45, reached 50% NH3 conversion (T50) at 422 °C, compared to 600 °C for Ru and 600 °C for bimetallic Co-Mo.; The apparent activation energy (Eapp) varied from 64.7 kJ mol−1 for the most active HEA-Co25Mo45 to 123.1 kJ mol−1 for the least active HEA-Co55Mo15.; Nitrogen desorption energy (ΔEN) for HEA-Co25Mo45 was ~79 kJ mol−1, which is very close to the value for Ru (84 kJ mol−1).; Catalytic activity exhibited a volcano-type behavior with respect to nitrogen adsorption energy, peaking at an optimal ΔEN of ~79 kJ mol−1.; The HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst showed negligible degradation after ~50 hours of continuous operation at 500 °C.; For pure NH3 decomposition, HEA-Co55Mo15 achieved an improvement factor of ~118 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~40 versus Ru.; Atomistic modeling confirmed a single solid-solution phase with δ = 5.4% and ΔHmix = 0.65 kJ mol−1, showing no phase segregation up to 1000 K.. Mechanism: The high catalytic activity is attributed to the robust tuning of surface nitrogen binding strength via the Co/Mo ratio; the optimal activity arises from a tradeoff where Co-rich catalysts bind N too weakly (limiting dehydrogenation) and Mo-rich catalysts bind N too strongly (limiting N2 desorption), with the HEA composition allowing access to the optimal intermediate binding energy (~79 kJ mol−1) predicted by the Sabatier principle.. Limitations: The text notes that the peak intensities in XRD patterns are low due to the much smaller particle sizes compared to previously reported HEAs, and that the bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts are constrained by large miscibility gaps in their phase diagram.. Future work: The authors propose designing practical reactors with cascaded catalyst layers having gradually changing nitrogen binding strengths to match the varying concentration of NH3 along the flow, which can be readily achieved by varying the Co/Mo ratios in HEA catalysts.. Quote: "Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram."

card: Paper card. Question: How can multi-elemental alloy nanoparticles (MEA-NPs) composed of traditionally immiscible elements be rationally designed and rapidly synthesized to achieve high catalytic efficiency and durability for ammonia decomposition?. System: RuRhCoNi (Ru-4 MEA-NPs) and RuRhCoNiIr (Ru-5 MEA-NPs) nanoparticles; precursor elements: Ru, Rh, Co, Ni, Ir, Pd, Cr, Fe, Cu, Mo. Processing: Rapid high-temperature synthesis via electrical Joule heating: multi-elemental salt precursors (0.05 M in ethanol) deposited on activated carbon nanofibers, heated to 1500 K for 500 ms (0.5 s), followed by quenching. Test conditions: Catalytic NH3 decomposition in a fixed-bed flow reactor at atmospheric pressure; gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) ≥30,000; reaction temperatures stepped from 300°C to 550°C; in situ stability testing in electron microscope up to 873 K for 30 min per point. Findings: Ru-4 MEA-NPs reached 100% NH3 decomposition at ~470°C, whereas a pure Ru sample with similar loading showed only 30% conversion.; MEA-NPs exhibited an ultrasmall and uniform particle size distribution of ~3 to 5 nm.; Ru atoms in Ru-5 MEA-NPs diffuse approximately 100 times slower than in a binary Ru-Ni alloy, indicating sluggish diffusion.; The Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintained a homogeneous alloy structure and uniform dispersion after in situ annealing up to 873 K.; Ru-5 MEA-NPs outperformed a Ru-5 sample prepared by impregnation (annealed at 300°C for 1 hour), confirming the alloy structure's role in performance.; The alloy formation temperature for Ru-Ni bimetallic is ~2000 K, while it decreases to 871 K for Ru-4 and 584 K for Ru-5 MEA-NPs due to entropy effects.; MEA-NPs showed a fragmented domain structure with rich interfaces, unlike the single domain structure of pure Ru NPs.. Mechanism: Entropy-driven thermodynamic stabilization (increased mixing entropy lowers Gibbs free energy) combined with kinetic stabilization (sluggish diffusion caused by lattice distortion and atomic size mismatch) prevents phase separation and elemental segregation, enabling the formation of uniform alloy structures from immiscible elements.. Limitations: DFT calculations did not account for vibrational energy and surface-energy effects in nanoparticles, meaning predicted formation temperatures represent a thermodynamic lower limit; short-range chemical ordering exists, meaning the alloy is not completely random.. Future work: The computationally aided rational design and rapid synthesis method can be generally used to accelerate catalyst discovery in multi-elemental materials for various catalytic reactions.. Quote: "We report the computationally aided, entropy-driven design and synthesis of highly efficient and durable catalyst MEA-NPs."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the type and number of elements in Ni-based single-phase equiatomic alloys affect their electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, particularly regarding the role of chemical and magnetic disorder?. System: Eight Ni-based FCC equiatomic alloys: elemental Ni, NiCo, NiFe, NiCoFe, NiCoCr, NiCoFeCr, NiCoFeCrMn, and NiCoFeCrPd. Processing: Arc-melting of pure elemental metals (>99.9% pure) followed by five flips and re-melts, drop-casting into a copper mold, and conversion to single crystals or polycrystalline rods via optical floating zone furnace; samples cut to ~1 × 1 × 10 mm3 and electrolytically polished. Test conditions: Electrical resistivity and thermal conductivity measured from 4 to 300 K; magnetization measured in magnetic fields up to 4 T from 4 to 300 K. Findings: Resistivities of alloys containing Cr (e.g., NiCoCr, NiCoFeCr) are about one order of magnitude larger than those without Cr (e.g., NiCoFe, NiFe).; The residual resistivity does not strongly correlate with the number of elements; the addition of Cr rapidly increases resistivity while Co has limited effects.; Thermal conductivities of the alloys are largely lower than pure metals primarily because high electrical resistivity suppresses the electronic thermal conductivity.; In concentrated alloys, lattice thermal conductivity (κg) dominates at low temperatures and is comparable to electronic thermal conductivity (κe) at room temperature.; The NiCoFeCrMn alloy exhibits a resistivity minimum at ~25 K, suggesting Kondo-like behavior or a spin glass transition.; NiCoCr is paramagnetic above 4 K, while NiCoFeCr has a Curie temperature (Tc) of ~120 K.; The addition of Cr significantly reduces magnetization due to magnetic cancellation, as Cr moments are anti-parallel to Ni, Co, and Fe moments.. Mechanism: High residual resistivity in alloys containing Cr and Mn is strongly attributed to magnetic disorder, where the presence of antiferromagnetically coupled elements (Cr, Mn) alongside ferromagnetically coupled elements (Ni, Co, Fe) creates strong scattering potentials for both spin-up and spin-down electrons, shortening the electron mean-free-path.. Limitations: The KKR-CPA calculations neglect displacement fluctuations, which may contribute to residual resistivity, particularly in alloys with large atomic size mismatches like NiCoFeCrPd.. Future work: Further studies are needed to investigate the origin of the finite positive TCR at low temperatures in NiCoCr, and additional experiments (ac susceptibility, heat capacity, neutron scattering) are required to conclusively determine the nature of the transition near 25 K in NiCoFeCrMn.. Quote: "The scattering of electrons is significantly increased due to the chemical (especially magnetic) disorder."
